Newborn Care

Breastfeeding: A Beginner’s Guide

Updated: July 1, 2026

Breastfeeding is natural, but that does not mean it comes naturally , it is a learned skill for both you and your baby. Most early challenges are common and solvable, especially with good support. Here is a gentle, realistic guide to the first weeks.

Getting started in the first days

The first milk your body makes is colostrum: thick, golden, and produced in small amounts perfectly matched to a newborn’s tiny stomach. Frequent feeding in the first days tells your body to build supply, so early and often is the theme.

Around day two to five, your milk typically "comes in" and volumes increase noticeably. Skin-to-skin contact and unrestricted feeding during this period help everything get established.

Latch basics

A good latch is the foundation of comfortable feeding. Aim for your baby to take a big mouthful of breast , not just the nipple , with lips flanged outward and chin touching the breast. Bringing baby to breast (rather than leaning toward baby) helps.

A deep latch should not be persistently painful. Brief tenderness in the first seconds can happen early on, but ongoing pain, pinching, or damaged nipples usually mean the latch needs adjusting , a fixable problem, not a personal failing.

How often and how long

Newborns typically breastfeed eight to twelve times in 24 hours, sometimes in clusters , several feeds close together, often in the evening. Cluster feeding is normal and helps build your supply; it is not a sign you have too little milk.

Feed on cue rather than by the clock: rooting, hand-sucking, and stirring all say "feed me soon." Let your baby finish the first breast before offering the second, since the milk changes in composition through a feed.

Common early challenges

Sore nipples are usually a latch issue , adjusting position and depth often resolves them. Expressed milk or lanolin on the nipples after feeds can soothe while things heal.

Engorgement , breasts feeling overly full, hard, and tender when milk comes in , usually eases with frequent feeding, gentle massage, and warmth before feeds or cool compresses after. If a hard, painful area appears with fever or flu-like feelings, contact your provider, as that can signal mastitis, which is treatable.

How to know baby is getting enough

You cannot see the milliliters, but you can see the outputs: by around day five, expect roughly six or more wet diapers a day and regular stools that transition from dark and tarry to yellow and seedy.

Other reassuring signs: you can hear or see swallowing during feeds, your baby seems settled after many feeds, and weight returns to birth weight within about two weeks. Your pediatrician tracks this at checkups , never hesitate to ask how things look.

Where to get support

Lactation consultants exist precisely because breastfeeding is a skill with a learning curve. A single session can transform a painful latch or a fussy feeder , many hospitals, clinics, and community programs offer access to one.

Support also comes from postpartum nurses, midwives, breastfeeding drop-in groups, and experienced friends. Asking for help early , before small problems grow , is the single best predictor of a smoother experience.

Key takeaways

  • Breastfeeding is a learned skill , early challenges are common and usually solvable.
  • A deep latch (big mouthful, lips flanged) is the key to comfortable feeding.
  • Expect 8–12 feeds in 24 hours; cluster feeding is normal and builds supply.
  • Wet diapers, swallowing sounds, and weight gain show baby is getting enough.
  • See a lactation consultant early for pain or latch trouble , it makes a real difference.

Frequently asked questions

Is breastfeeding supposed to hurt?

Persistent pain is not something to push through , it usually signals a shallow latch or positioning issue. A lactation consultant can often fix it in one visit, so seek help early.

How do I know my baby is getting enough milk?

Track diapers and weight rather than guessing: about six or more wet diapers a day by day five, regular stools, and a return to birth weight by around two weeks are the classic reassuring signs.

What is cluster feeding and is it normal?

Cluster feeding is several feeds bunched close together, often in the evening or during growth spurts. It is completely normal newborn behavior and helps signal your body to make more milk.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
